agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: The full scan confirms that layers 10, 11 and 12 up_proj are the strongest coordinated groups in the model, with 34, 38 and 39 rows at |cos| > 0.4 to the shared direction. Other MLP layers have at most about 20, except layer 25 with 99. The attention-matrix numbers are high everywhere, so they reflect natural low-dimensional structure rather than an anomaly. To decide how to undo the group, I need to know whether the planted neurons are new, dedicated units or natural neurons with a v0 component added to their up rows (row ← row + c·v0). In the first case they would be zeroed; in the second, v0 would be projected out of those rows. I will look at the distribution of the up-row projections on v0 in each of the three layers. A clearly separated cluster with one sign and a consistent size would indicate an added component, and its size relative to the rest of the row would show how much of each neuron is natural.

The projections settle it. In every layer, 99% of up rows have |projection on v0| below about 0.12, but about 30 to 40 rows sit at ±0.8 to ±1.4, with both signs. Their remaining (orthogonal) part has an ordinary norm, about 0.76 to 1.05 against a median near 1. This looks like natural neurons with a large ±c·v0 component added to their up rows. So the most surgical undo is to remove that component from those rows rather than delete the neurons. I will build edit E2: in layers 10, 11 and 12, for rows with |proj| > 0.3, subtract the projection on that layer's own top singular direction, setting the component to zero. I will then test it with a paired generation pass on DEV[:256]. If these rows carry the suppression, accuracy should rise clearly, beyond the roughly 3-point standard error. If accuracy does not move, the group is either natural or not the cause, and I will try full ablation next.

Edit E2 is saved. It removes the v0 component from 45, 39 and 46 up-rows in layers 10, 11 and 12 respectively, and nothing else changes. I am running a paired generation pass ("both") on DEV[:256] to see whether removing this planted component raises accuracy. A gain of more than about 6 points (two standard errors) would support the hypothesis that this group suppresses math ability. No change would mean these rows are not the bottleneck, at least not in this form.

E2 hurt slightly: −3.1 ± 1.7 points, with only 18 of 256 answers changing in either direction. Removing the planted v0 component from the layer 10 to 12 up rows has little effect and does not unlock anything. Either the group is a decoy or natural, or v0 is rarely present in the inputs, so the planted part seldom matters. I will put E2 aside, drop it so that later measurements start from the original, and look for other kinds of suppression. Candidates are norm weights that change attention sharpness (q_norm/k_norm) or the layer scales, and heads or near-constant units that write a fixed "weak mode" vector. As a cheap weight-only check, I will compare q_norm/k_norm weights across layers. I will also check the post-attention and post-FFN norm weights for single dimensions with extreme values that differ from neighbouring layers. Separately, I will check how accuracy depends on problem difficulty, measured as the number of reference steps, to see whether the model fails even on one- or two-step problems.
